title: Trump Says Putin Wants a Deal More Than Zelenskyy, Presses Kyiv to Settle
excerpt: The president defended his disputed energy-ceasefire claim and put the onus on Ukraine's leader, while Kyiv reported fresh Russian strikes and European leaders publicly backed Zelenskyy.
body:
• President Donald Trump said Vladimir Putin "wants to make a deal more than Zelensky," pressing Ukraine's president to settle as he defended his claim that both sides agreed to an energy ceasefire.
  • Neither Moscow nor Kyiv has publicly confirmed that ceasefire; Zelenskyy says Russia struck a Kyiv apartment building with a Shahed drone, killing two people and injuring nine.
  • Trump put the war's toll at 32,000 people lost "this month" — his figure, offered without supporting detail — and said the two leaders "have to get together and end that ridiculous war."
  • European leaders publicly backed Zelenskyy after he called Trump's Russian diesel deal "weak," setting up a widening gap between Washington's pressure on Kyiv and Europe's pressure on Moscow.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Russian President Vladimir Putin appeared more willing than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reach a peace agreement, pressing Kyiv to settle even as questions mounted over alleged Russian violations of the energy ceasefire Trump announced a day earlier. "I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky," Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for a political rally in Ohio, according to IANS.

"Zelensky and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war."

— Donald Trump, US President

A ceasefire only one side describes

On Sunday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks against each other's energy infrastructure. Neither government has publicly confirmed it. Asked how he would persuade Putin to abide by the proposal, Trump again emphasised securing Zelenskyy's agreement: "What's happening is he wants to make a deal, and we have to get Zelensky to want to make a deal." Challenged on his claim that an agreement existed at all, he stood by it: "They agreed because I said they agreed and that thing has to get settled."

https://x.com/atrupar/status/2109753188945465857

Ukraine's account of the same hours is different. Zelenskyy posted that Russia had struck a high-rise apartment building in Kyiv with a Shahed drone, killing two people and injuring nine, and accused Moscow of continuing its terror against civilians. In Kharkiv, a Russian drone strike on a residential area injured at least 12 people, including a child, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service. The Videshi reported the first of these strikes in our coverage of the ceasefire announcement and its immediate aftermath.

The diesel deal behind the friction

The exchange follows Trump's agreement allowing large quantities of Russian diesel onto international markets — a move Zelenskyy publicly called a "weak decision," arguing it gives Putin money that is spent on the war. Trump responded by accusing Zelenskyy of disregarding his instructions not to attack Russian refineries, warning that such strikes worsen fuel shortages, and suggesting Ukraine needed a leader willing to compromise. European leaders closed ranks behind Kyiv instead: Berlin's foreign minister said Germany "fully supports" Zelenskyy and called for increased pressure on Putin, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen echoed the backing, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham assured Ukraine of his "complete solidarity," according to Le Monde.

What it means

The pattern now is consistent: Washington's leverage is being applied most visibly to Kyiv, while Europe's is aimed at Moscow. Trump provided no details of any formal understanding between the two countries, nor how a ceasefire would be monitored or enforced. For energy markets — and for Indian buyers of diesel and crude watching prices already distorted by the Middle East war — the gap between the announced ceasefire and the reported strikes is the fact that matters.

What's next

Watch for any public statement from Moscow or Kyiv confirming terms, and for whether US pressure produces a Ukrainian negotiating concession or a European counter-package of support. Until one side confirms the energy ceasefire in its own words, it remains an announcement, not an agreement.
